transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dan Ronin.
Flights at U.S. airlines are gradually resuming after a nationwide groundstrop that the Trump
administration says was caused by an overload of older technology used at older air traffic
control facilities.
Tens of thousands of passengers are being impacted at hundreds of airports by one of
the biggest aviation disruptions in decades.
NPR's Joel Rose reports that getting all of the people impacted by the groundstop to their
destination could take days as airlines reschedule flights and rebook the passengers.
Captain officials, including the DOT Secretary Sean Duffy, are explaining what happened.
When reporters pushed and asked for clarity on exactly what went wrong, he wasn't able
to give them a whole lot of specifics.
He pivoted again and again to pushing for more money to rebuild the nation's air traffic
control system, which has been a big priority for this administration, but we still have
only Duffy's word that this was the old year that failed.
We don't have a lot of detail on what it was.
A number of flights are departing and arriving passengers are being told to contact their
airlines.
Lawmakers on Capitol Hill say they still want the former CEO of NVIDIA to testify regarding
his alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy from member station WCMU.
A.J.
Jones reports.
Republican Congressman John Molinar represents mid-Michigan and chairs the House Select Committee
on the Chinese Communist Party.
He says he has several questions for Jensen Huang.
Is there privileged information that was shared with a Chinese spy?
What kind of influence did the Chinese intelligence operative have with respect to national security
policy?
Huang's resignation followed news reports that Huang had an extramarital affair with
one of the company's clients.
The woman is suspected of having been recruited by China's top spy agency, an allegation that
NPR has not independently confirmed.
For NPR News, I'm AJ Jones.
The man accused of trying to assassinate President Trump during last spring's White House correspondence
dinner is facing new indictment.
NPR's Ryan Lucas says that Cole Allen faces five additional counts.
The new indictment adds one count of committing an act of terrorism while armed.
That's in addition to the other counts Cole Allen was already facing, including trying
to assassinate President Trump.
He has pleaded not guilty.
Others say Allen traveled from Los Angeles to Washington, D.C., and booked a room in
the same hotel where the White House Correspondents' Dinner was taking place in April.
He then allegedly tried to storm the dinner with a shotgun and other weapons to kill President
Trump, but was stopped by Secret Service agents at the outer perimeter.
Ryan Lucas, NPR News, Washington.
Stocks closed the week mix, the Dow was up, the S&P and NASDAQ were off, it's NPR.
Pope Leo is back in his former country that he lived in, Peru, as he continues in his
Latin American trip, telling Catholics, "It is a joy to return to that nation."
The Vatican estimates that one million people lined the Pope's motorcade and another half
million were at a mass where he later served for two decades as a missionary priest and
a bishop before being elevated to Cardinal and later Pope.
A Kansas district attorney says he will not file charges against the driver in a deadly
crash at a Wichita soccer field last month.
Roger Noemmer of member station KMUW has more.
Two people died and 10 others were injured in the crash at the crowded soccer field last
month.
Sedgwick County District Attorney Mark Bennett says a police investigation determined the
driver, a 34-year-old woman from Garden City, was asleep at the time of the crash and did
not act with intent or recklessness.
He says part of his job is to hold people accountable when he can prove they committed
a crime.
I am also charged, also required, also it is my solemn responsibility to stand before
the community and say as bad as this was, it is not a crime.
Police interviewed more than 100 witnesses and reviewed at least 60 videos from the scene.
For NPR News, I'm Roger Noemmer in Wichita.
The Family Dollar Company says it will pay a $63 million settlement this after it was
sued by the Federal Trade Commission in several states.
They allege the company routinely charged customers more at the cash register than those
prices displayed.
I'm Dan Roman, NPR.

topics.text: Airline groundstop caused by overloaded old air traffic control technology, Duffy says, with few details
Lawmakers want former NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang to testify about alleged ties to suspected Chinese spy
Cole Allen faces five new counts, including terrorism while armed, over alleged White House Correspondents' Dinner attack
Pope Leo returns to Peru, drawing huge crowds to motorcade and mass in former mission region
Wichita district attorney Mark Bennett declines charges against driver in fatal soccer field crash
Family Dollar to pay $63 million settlement over charging customers more than displayed prices
